cues.text: Let us turn now to the ninth chapter, where we apply the MIND CA approach to a very practical question: what happens to people, and what happens to customers, when an organisation changes the way it builds and delivers technology?
The case we use here is MTN, and the section is titled "MIND CA application: people and customer impact." Start with the problem the case describes.
MTN's case points to two connected symptoms: handoffs across teams, and slow releases.
Think about what a handoff is.
One team finishes its part of the work and passes it to another team, which then picks it up, interprets it, does its own part, and passes it on again.
Every handoff is a point where work waits in a queue, where information can be lost, and where nobody feels fully responsible for the end result.
When a release, meaning a new version of a product or service going live, has to travel through many such handoffs, it naturally becomes slow.
So the slow releases are not a separate issue.
They are the visible result of the handoffs.
The source then offers two organisational responses.
The first is cross-functional squads.
A squad is a small team that brings together the different skills needed to deliver a piece of work, rather than splitting those skills into separate departments.
The source states that cross-functional squads reduce organisational silos.
A silo is a part of an organisation that works in isolation, with its own priorities, its own language and little connection to the others.
When people with different skills sit in one squad, they talk directly, decide together, and the number of handoffs falls.
The second response is platform engineering.
The source says platform engineering standardises delivery.
In plain terms, instead of every team building and releasing its work in its own way, a platform provides a common, consistent way to build, test and deliver.
Standardisation means squads do not reinvent the same tooling each time, and delivery becomes more predictable.
Notice how the two ideas fit together: squads give autonomy and shared ownership, while the platform gives a common foundation so that autonomy does not turn into chaos.
Now we come to the people side, which the source treats as a matter of change management.
It says change management must address four things.
First, retraining.
People who have worked in one way for years need to learn new skills and new practices.
Second, ownership.
In a squad model, it must be clear who owns what, because the old boundaries between departments are changing.
Third, security responsibilities.
When delivery is shared across a squad and runs on a common platform, people need to understand what part of security is theirs, rather than assuming that some other team will handle it.
And fourth, fear of new practices.
The source names this explicitly.
People may worry about their roles, about making mistakes in unfamiliar ways of working, or about being left behind.

A good lecturer would say plainly that this fear is not a side issue to be ignored; it is something change management must address directly, or the new structure will exist on paper but not in behaviour.
The source also recommends how to move: a gradual migration.
The reasoning is given in two parts.
A gradual migration protects customer journeys, meaning the sequence of steps a customer goes through to get something done, such as sending money or buying airtime.
If an organisation changed everything at once, a mistake could break those journeys for many customers together.
And a gradual migration allows learning, because the organisation can move one part, see what works and what does not, and adjust before moving the next.
Finally, the source turns to the customer, and to a particularly sensitive situation: financial requests that run into outages.
An outage is a period when a system or part of it is not working properly.
The source says customers need accurate pending, success and failure states.
Let us be clear about the three.
Pending means the request has been received but its outcome is not yet known.
Success means it was completed.
Failure means it was not completed.
The key word is accurate: the customer must be shown what is truly known, not a guess.
If the system does not yet know the outcome, saying pending is honest, whereas wrongly saying failure or success is not.
The source closes with a specific warning.
Retrying an ambiguous transfer without reconciliation can undermine trust.
An ambiguous transfer is one where, after an outage, it is unclear whether the money actually moved.
Reconciliation means checking the records on the relevant sides to establish what really happened.
If a system simply retries the transfer without doing that check, it may repeat something that already succeeded.
The source does not spell out the exact consequence, but it states the effect that matters for this chapter: trust in the service can be undermined.

So, bringing the chapter together in its original order: handoffs and slow releases are the problem; cross-functional squads and platform engineering are the organisational response; change management must cover retraining, ownership, security responsibilities and fear of new practices;

gradual migration protects customer journeys and enables learning; and when outages hit financial requests, customers need accurate pending, success and failure states, with reconciliation before any retry of an ambiguous transfer.
